name: Antares
intro: This is the bottom half of Antares, which landed Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell in the Fra Mauro hills on 5 February 1971, the target Apollo 13 never reached. When the crew left, it stayed behind as their launch pad.

hotspots.title: A speck of solder
hotspots.text: Before landing, the computer kept seeing the abort button as pressed. That could have made it fire this engine to climb back to orbit instead of landing. A loose speck of solder in the switch was probably to blame, and engineers on Earth quickly worked out a fix.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Landing at Fra Mauro

hotspots.title: Golf on the Moon
hotspots.text: Near here, Shepard fixed a golf club head to the handle of a sampling tool and hit two golf balls. Swinging one-handed in a stiff spacesuit, he still sent them flying across the dust.

hotspots.title: The plaque
hotspots.text: A plaque on the ladder leg carries the crew’s signatures and a map of Earth’s two halves. It will stay readable for a very long time, since there is no wind or rain to wear it away.

photo.alt: A shiny metal plaque with two round maps of Earth and the words Apollo 14 Antares.
photo.caption: The Apollo 14 plaque, photographed on Earth before launch.

hotspots.title: Antares on the Moon
hotspots.text: Antares brought home 42 kg of rock, including broken-up pieces thought to be thrown out by the giant impact that made the Imbrium basin.

photo.alt: The lunar module stands on the grey ground with a bright starburst of sunlight above it.
photo.caption: Antares on 5 February 1971; the ball of light is the Sun reflecting in the camera lens.

hotspots.title: The missing top half
hotspots.text: The crew cabin sat here. On 6 February 1971 it fired its engine and flew back to orbit, using this bottom half as a launch pad.

funFact: Alan Shepard, the first American in space, was 47 years old here, the oldest person ever to walk on the Moon.
whyLeft: Nothing broke: the bottom half was designed to be left as a launch pad when the cabin flew back to orbit.
repurpose: Its tanks are empty, but it is a perfect time capsule: close-up photos from a future rover could show how 50 years of sunlight and tiny meteorites changed its gold foil.
